Pronounced “pa-vay,” pavé originates from the French word “to pave” — in this case, as in paved with diamonds. In a pavé setting, small diamonds line the band. The metal prongs or beads that hold the diamonds in place are barely visible.

The pavé setting adds extra sparkle to an engagement, all while emphasizing the beauty of the center diamond. Pavé settings are available in a wide range of styles, from modern settings to a range of vintage designs that incorporate pavé-set diamonds.

Diamonds are pavé set when they’re as small as .01-.02 carats. Diamonds smaller than that are considered micro-pavé (which are usually set in thin bands).

Ver | SA-ce ver | SA-ce me | DU-sa head | ON me like | I’m ‘lu-min | NA-ti — |

line: Yeah
meaning:
The opening “yeah” from Quavo in the song Fly With a Fish might seem simple, but it signifies his presence, confidence, and personal growth. This single-word ad-lib acts like a ceremonial spark before the verse starts. In hip-hop, especially in Atlanta trap music, an opening ad-lib often carries meaning beyond the literal, and Quavo’s “yeah” is no different.

By this stage in his career, Quavo had already made his mark as the melodic heart of Migos. His voice became linked with luxury, ambition, and smooth flows that blended rapping and melody. So when he enters the track with a calm, confident “yeah,” it shows the comfort of an artist who doesn’t need to force attention anymore. Earlier in Migos’ journey, the group relied on explosive energy and quick delivery to prove themselves. Now, Quavo sounds relaxed—almost effortless. That “yeah” symbolizes someone who understands his status even before the beat kicks in.

There’s also a deeper meaning connected to the title “Fly With a Fish.” Fish traditionally symbolize survival, adaptability, and movement in tough environments. A fish survives underwater, handling pressure and darkness naturally. By starting the song with “yeah,” Quavo subtly acknowledges how he has survived the music industry in a similar manner. The word quietly affirms everything he has faced: poverty, criticism, competition, and fame. It is less of an introduction and more of a recognition, like someone reflecting on their journey and saying, “I really made it here.”

Some listeners see the ad-lib’s delivery as emotionally distant, but that detachment might be intentional. In modern trap music, emotional restraint often conveys strength. Quavo doesn’t shout the word or dramatize it because he no longer seeks validation. The understated “yeah” reflects a veteran mindset. It conveys the vibe of someone who has become so familiar with success that confidence sounds casual.

Musically, the “yeah” also sets the rhythm before any actual lyrics start. Quavo has always treated ad-libs as instruments rather than just filler. The timing, tone, and texture of the word prepare the listener for the song’s mood. It acts almost like a producer tag for his personality. Before he raps a single line, the listener already knows the world they’re entering: luxury, street wisdom, ambition, and calm dominance.

Moreover, some argue that the “yeah” conveys the weariness of fame. Quavo’s delivery isn’t overly excited; it’s controlled and almost introspective. After years of commercial success, public attention, and endless recording, that one-word opening can be seen as the voice of someone who has experienced everything the industry has to offer. Instead of youthful excitement, there’s a sense of maturity in how he says it. The word carries the weight of experience.

In Atlanta rap culture, ad-libs often signal identity. Artists like Future, Young Thug, and Migos have turned ad-libs into emotional expressions. Quavo’s “yeah” aligns with that tradition. It isn’t meant to be analyzed literally; its meaning comes from tone, placement, and presence. The reason it feels powerful despite its simplicity is that listeners subconsciously associate his voice with years of cultural impact and success.

Ultimately, the opening “yeah” is a brief summary of Quavo’s artistic identity. It represents confidence without needing explanation, survival without complaints, and status without effort. In just one syllable, he suggests that the song has already started emotionally before it even begins lyrically.

line: Got so many Ks, Confederate
vault_lines: Got so many Ks, Confederate
meaning:
“K” is a letter used to alude to money, specifically one thousand dollars. This is derived from the prefix “kilo-” which is used to quantify things in the thousands, such as one kilometer, which is one thousand meters.

Although at the surface level this is simply another typical braggadocious line from Takeoff, he post-modifies his “Ks” with the word “Confederate,” which references the Confederate States of America. These were a group of breakaway states in Southern USA between February 1861 and May 1865, amidst the American Civil War.

The seven states who formed the Confederacy did so due to disagreements about the use of slave labor, as the economy of these states was heavily reliant on the existence of slavery, which the rest of the Nation was fighting to abolish. Therefore, it is fair to deem the Confederates as a racist group, due to their disdain for African Americans.

Takeoff, therefore, uses the presumptuous racism of Confederates to compare them to the Ku Klux Klan, or the ‘KKK’ – hence “so many Ks.” The KKK is a group of white supremacists founded as a result of the Confederacy’s failure in the civil war.



Pictured: A KKK member carrying a  Confederate flag at a 2015 rally

meaning:
In this line, Takeoff employs a double meaning of sorts. By saying that he can “Do a trick with the stick”, he references the stereotypical stage magician, who performs magic tricks on stage with a wand. In this interpretation, a magic wand is the “stick” that Takeoff speaks of.

By making this statement, Takeoff compares himself and the rest of the Migos to magicians; he implies that they create high-quality music that others cannot parallel, thus putting them in the same tier of respect/talent as magicians. This falls in line with the theme of the song, as the title “Straightenin” is repeated dozens of times throughout the chorus and verses. A magician’s wand is straight like a rod, making it a perfect object of comparison for Takeoff in a song called “Straightenin”.



Additionally, this line carries a more sinister meaning for those who consider the multiple interpretations of the lyric. “Stick” is a slang term for a long firearm (like an AK-47), which causes the line to carry a much different interpretation of the phrase “Do a trick with the stick”. In this sense, the “trick” that Takeoff implies he can do with his gun is that of making a human disappear, or, to put it bluntly, shooting someone to death.



He compares himself and his band members to magicians with magic wands, except their magic wands come in the form of firearms and their signature magic trick is gunning down those who oppose them.

meaning:
Pavé is a type of engagement ring setting which the shank of the ring is lined with small diamonds. These diamonds are held in place with metal prongs or beads, creating the appearance of a line of continuous small diamonds.



Pronounced “pa-vay,” pavé originates from the French word “to pave” — in this case, as in paved with diamonds. In a pavé setting, small diamonds line the band. The metal prongs or beads that hold the diamonds in place are barely visible.

The pavé setting adds extra sparkle to an engagement, all while emphasizing the beauty of the center diamond. Pavé settings are available in a wide range of styles, from modern settings to a range of vintage designs that incorporate pavé-set diamonds.

Diamonds are pavé set when they’re as small as .01-.02 carats. Diamonds smaller than that are considered micro-pavé (which are usually set in thin bands).

And Cartier is a French luxury goods conglomerate which designs, manufactures, distributes, and sells jewellery and watches. Founded by Louis-François Cartier in Paris in 1847. He says that he pavéd his pairs.

Having finally been granted bail on December 4, 2015 and still somewhat fresh off release, Offset was asked to describe how it felt to have been arrested for a second time in a 2016 The FADER interview:

It felt like I was taking a step back because I’m not in the streets no more. I was doing the right thing, helping my family, and supporting my family with the music. And for me to go back to jail, I was in there thinking like, “Damn, what did I do?” And at first I was lost, because I ain’t had no understanding of how you can go from being on the top to right there in that situation so quick. When I got my mind right, I was just like, “Maybe this is God telling me what I need to do.” Or it could be saving me? It could be so many reasons why I had to do what I had to do. But it was a hard time, though. Everything was going on and now you just sitting still.
